summary: Provides a framework and a template for writing specifications of services that network elements offer to applications in networks with multiple qualities of service. It gives context, definitions and suggested data formats, then sets out the template that service documents should follow.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2216 gives service designers a shared vocabulary and a template for describing network quality-of-service capabilities. It explains what information each service description should provide so network elements and setup protocols can use it.

subtitle: A framework and template for describing quality-of-service services in network elements.

tldr.problem: Specifications for network services need shared terms and a consistent description of what each network element does and what applications can expect.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2216 defines service, flow, traffic and request specifications, then gives a template for describing packet handling, parameters, exported information, policing, ordering and evaluation.
tldr.outcome: The memo provides a format for service specifications; it does not define a particular quality-of-service service or setup protocol.

today: RFC 2216 is an Informational framework for writing network-element service specifications. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: What the Template Describes
sections.content:
The RFC defines a framework for describing services offered by routers, switches, subnetworks and other network elements. A service description states what the element does, what information it needs, what information it exports and what behavior results when services along a path are combined.

The document does not define the protocols that establish state in network elements. It focuses on the service's requirements and the interfaces between the service and its environment.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains how to describe a network service, rather than defining one specific service. The description covers what a network element needs, what it does and what it tells other parts of the network.

sections.title: Flows, Requests and Traffic
sections.content:
A flow is a set of packets covered by the same request for quality-of-service control at a network element. A service is a coordinated set of capabilities provided by one element. The resulting end-to-end behavior comes from combining the services along the packet path.

The Traffic Specification (TSpec) describes the allowed traffic pattern. The Service Request Specification (RSpec) describes the requested quality of service, such as bandwidth, delay or packet loss. The service's promise applies while the flow stays within the traffic described by its TSpec.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic specification (TSpec) describes the traffic a network element should expect. The service request specification (RSpec) describes the quality of service an application asks for.

sections.title: Characterization and Composition
sections.content:
A network element may export characterization parameters, such as available bandwidth or estimated delay. A composition function combines these values from multiple elements to estimate end-to-end behavior. The RFC says every defined parameter needs a rule for how it is composed across the path.

Characterizations may not be available at every element, especially when a path uses different services. The RFC therefore describes a validity flag: an element that cannot provide a parameter marks the result invalid while leaving its value unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Network elements can report measurements or estimates about their part of a path. A setup or routing mechanism can combine those reports, while a validity flag shows when information is missing.

sections.title: Parameters and Numbering
sections.content:
A service specification must define the abstract format of each data item, including its type, range and precision. It should also give a preferred concrete packet format when useful. This gives protocol designers enough information to carry the data.

Services and their parameters use a two-level number space: service_name.parameter_name. Service number 1 is generic, numbers 2 through 127 are for IETF-defined services, and numbers above 127 through 254 are reserved for experimental or private services. Zero and 255 are reserved. Parameter numbers have a per-service range with shared and service-specific values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each service description needs to say what its values mean, how large they can be and how precise they must be. Numbers identify services and their parameters so different protocols can refer to the same item.

sections.title: Required Service Description Sections
sections.content:
A service specification must include sections for end-to-end behavior, motivation, network-element data handling, invocation information, exported information, policing, ordering and merging, and evaluation criteria. The template also lists optional sections for implementer guidance and examples of implementation and use.

The required sections distinguish normative requirements from explanatory material. For example, the policing section describes what happens when a flow exceeds its traffic specification and where the network detects that mismatch. Evaluation criteria describe tests that can compare implementations on a single network element.
sections.plainLanguage: A service description must explain why the service exists, what it does to packets, what information it uses and returns, and how it handles traffic outside the request. It also needs to say how an implementation can be evaluated.
